files.name: login.py

notes.8: Reads the `next` query parameter (where to go after login) — attacker-controlled.
notes.9: Redirects the browser to that value.

options.label: `redirect` issues a 302 that browsers don't cache
options.whyWrong: Caching is irrelevant to the redirect abuse.

options.label: The default of `/` means missing params break the flow
options.whyWrong: The default is a usability detail, not the vulnerability.

options.label: `next_url` is attacker-controlled and used as the redirect target, so a link to this trusted site can bounce victims to an attacker's site (phishing)
Reject next if it starts with 'http'
options.whyWrong: `//evil.com` (protocol-relative) and backslash tricks bypass this and still redirect off-site.

options.label: Allow only a local path: parse it and require an empty scheme and netloc
options.diff:
-    next_url = request.args.get("next", "/")
+    raw = request.args.get("next", "/")
+    u = urlparse(raw)
+    next_url = raw if (not u.scheme and not u.netloc and raw.startswith("/")) else "/"

options.label: URL-encode next_url before redirecting
options.whyWrong: Encoding corrupts a legitimate path and still can't confirm the destination is your site.

options.label: Check that next_url contains your domain name
options.whyWrong: `https://evil.com/?x=mysite.com` contains it; substring checks are trivially bypassed.

training.exploit: Send a victim `https://trusted/login?next=https://evil.example/` (or `next=//evil.example`). They log in on the real site and are redirected to an attacker page — often a convincing 'session expired, log in again' clone that harvests the credentials they just used.

hints.line: Where does user input choose where the browser goes?
hints.why: Who benefits from an off-site bounce on your trusted domain?
hints.fix: Permit only destinations within your own site.

writeup.summary: `redirect(next_url)` sends the browser wherever `next` points, including off-site. On a trusted domain this powers phishing: the victim trusts the first URL and lands on an attacker's clone. Restrict to local paths — parse the value and require an empty scheme and netloc (or use the framework's safe-URL helper). Blocklisting `http` misses protocol-relative and backslash forms.
